wine.name: Juan Gil Etiqueta Plata
wine.sites: Old, low yielding Monastrell vineyards of the family around Jumilla, on poor, chalky and stony limestone soils that suit the grape.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel tanks at a controlled temperature; after the malolactic fermentation the wine spends about twelve months in French oak barrels, the time set by each harvest, as the house's sheet tells it, before bottling.
wine.glass: Deep purple, near black; ripe currants, berries and smoke on the nose, then full and juicy in the mouth, with a long, spiced finish and the toast of its French oak.
wine.ageing: Bottled ready to drink after its year in oak, it is made to drink while its fruit is young, within a few years, and a ripe vintage keeps for several more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, inside the house's own 15 to 18; no need to decant; a large red wine glass, with grilled lamb.

label.means: Silver Label, the house's name for this Monastrell; abroad the bottle is sold as Silver Label.
The grape, the Mourvèdre of France; here it stands alone in the bottle.

records.table: Juan Gil Etiqueta Plata is the Jumilla house's Monastrell from old vines on poor limestone, given about a year in French oak and sold abroad as Silver Label. Dark, juicy and smoky, it is a red to pour with grilled lamb.
records.story: By the house's own account, its founder brought in his first harvest in the fields of Jumilla in 1916 and bottled his first wine that same year, and the bodega that carries his name is the first of the Gil family's wineries. The house was rooted in Monastrell, the grape of the town's own vineyards, from the start. In 2002 two brothers of the family's fourth generation took the company in hand again, as Hijos de Juan Gil, after one of them had spent two months going over its accounts, and the family dates a new era from that year. Etiqueta Plata is a wine of that era: Monastrell alone from the family's old vines on poor limestone, fermented in steel and given about twelve months in French oak, and by its importers' accounts the first wine of the new house, made from the 2002 vintage. Sold abroad as Silver Label, it became the bottle by which the family's name is known in other markets, and with the 2018 vintage, by the same accounts, its vineyards were certified organic. For a sommelier the Silver Label is a plain lesson in modern Jumilla: one grape, old vines and a year of French oak, made to be poured while its fruit is young.

others.name: Juan Gil Etiqueta Azul
others.note: The Blue Label: Monastrell with Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah, given eighteen months, mostly in oak, by the house's sheets.

traps: Etiqueta Plata and Silver Label are one wine, Monastrell alone; the Blue Label, Etiqueta Azul, is the blend with Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah.
The founder's first wine of 1916 and the family's new era of 2002 are different turning points: the Silver Label came with the second.

report: Searches for this record: 8 of the group's share of 35 (one of them on Bodegas El Nido), no fetch tried; the house's own pages were read through search on gilfamily.es, which the plan did not name.

The plan's note is answered: 1916 is the house's own year for the first harvest and the first bottled wine, and retailers give it too; the founder is named Juan Gil Giménez by the house and Juan Gil Jiménez by a merchant, and his dates were found nowhere, so he is described, not named.

The year 2002 rests on El Español (the brothers' refounding as Hijos de Juan Gil) and on importers' and merchants' pages (the Silver Label the first wine of the new era); the 2002 vintage of Juan Gil 12 Meses Silver Label is listed by Wine.com and Fine Wines International, so the label has been made from 2002.

The label words: Etiqueta Plata at home, Silver Label abroad, and Juan Gil 12 Meses on merchants' listings of older and some current vintages; 12 Meses is kept out of the label terms because no label image was read, and a Dutch merchant says the 2022 vintage first printed the name in both languages.

Left out for want of a second source or of room: the three weeks on the skins (two merchants, 20 to 25 days), the vines' age (forty, fifty or fifty two years by different merchants), dry farming (one importer), a new winery for the 2003 vintage (one merchant), the Etiqueta Amarilla, and the yield of the house's sheet.

Codex record in tension: the region record's producers line credits Juan Gil with the Cabernet led El Nido blends, but El Nido and Clio are wines of Bodegas El Nido, a separate Jumilla bodega the Gil family founded with partners in 2002 (Regal Wine Co, wine databases), as the plan's note says; the record leaves El Nido out rather than carry a trap on one importer's page.

Living people met and not named: the two brothers of the fourth generation who refounded the company in 2002 (named in El Español and by merchants), and an Australian winemaker named as a partner in El Nido; listed for the read together agent.

wine.name: Pie Franco
wine.grapes: Monastrell alone, from ungrafted vines on their own roots.
wine.sites: La Solana, a south facing plot of the estate planted in 1942, by the house's account, with Monastrell on its own roots in sandy soil.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented with native yeasts in stone lagares, with a share of whole bunches that changes from year to year; the malolactic fermentation follows in large oak foudres, and the wine then ages for well over a year in used French oak demi muids of 500 litres and in foudres.
wine.glass: A perfumed nose of liquorice, tobacco and an exotic spice over black and blue berries; in the mouth lively acidity and fine grained tannin, and a savoury rather than sweet finish.
wine.ageing: It gains from several years in bottle before it opens, and a good vintage keeps well beyond that.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a large Burgundy glass, which suits its perfume.

label.means: Own rooted: the vines are ungrafted, on their own roots rather than on an American rootstock.
The estate near Jumilla that the family's grandfather bought in 1941, and its winery.

records.table: Pie Franco is Casa Castillo's Monastrell from La Solana, a plot of ungrafted vines planted on sand near Jumilla in 1942. Fermented in stone lagares with some whole bunches and aged in large used oak, it is perfumed and fresh rather than heavy.
records.story: Wine was made on this land before the family came: an old winery and cellar stood on the estate, said to have been built in the 1870s by French growers fleeing phylloxera at home. In 1941, after the Civil War, the family's grandfather bought Casa Castillo and used it as a base for timber, esparto grass and aromatic herbs, and he began to plant small plots of vines, selling the grapes to bodegas nearby. One of those plots, La Solana, was planted in 1942 with Monastrell on its own roots in sand. In 1991, by the house's account, his son in law proposed bringing the disused winery back to life to make wine from the estate's own grapes, and the first wines of Casa Castillo followed. Two wines of single places came later: Las Gravas from a slope of deep gravel, and Pie Franco from La Solana, fermented in stone lagares and aged in large used oak. Pie Franco shows what old ungrafted Monastrell can give when it is handled lightly: perfume, fresh acidity and fine tannin. For a sommelier it is Jumilla's answer to the idea that Monastrell can only be heavy.

report: Searches for this record: 6 of the group's share of 35, no fetch tried; the house's own site was read through search on casacastillo.es.

The plan's note is answered: the house gives 1942 for the plot of Pie Franco and 1941 for the purchase of the estate; merchants give 1941 for the vines as well, so the record follows the house and names the other year in a trap.

Founded is empty: the estate was bought in 1941, an older winery is said to date from the 1870s, the house dates its own winemaking from a proposal of 1991, and importers give 1991 for the first vintage; no one year is the founding.

The French growers of the 1870s rest on two importers' and one magazine's pages, not on the house's, so the story tells them as said; the importers' replanting from 1985 and the grandson's arrival in 1994 rest on one source each and are left out.

Left out for want of a second source: the first vintage of Pie Franco and Las Gravas (1998, Spanish Wine Lover alone), the plot's size, the estate's height (up to 760 metres by one page, about 700 by another) and the share of whole bunches (30 to 50 or 40 to 60 per cent by vintage); the barrel time is well over a year because the sheets give 16 to 18 and 20 months.
The region record's producers line calls Casa Castillo the region's reference for site driven, fresher Monastrell; the record says only what the wine is and leaves the ranking out.
Living people met and not named: the grandson who runs the estate, and the buyer of 1941 and his wife, named by an importer, whose dates were not found; listed for the read together agent.

wine.name: Hécula
wine.sites: Old Monastrell of Campo Arriba, the high land north of Yecla at about 700 to 850 metres, on poor, stony limestone, Las Gruesas among the vineyards the house names.
wine.making: Picked by hand in late September and fermented in stainless steel tanks; the wine then spends a short time in French and American oak barrels, about six months by the house's account, before bottling.
wine.glass: Deep cherry red; ripe plum and blueberry over a toasted, balsamic background; delicate and silky in the mouth yet rich and well structured, with a long finish.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young, within a few years of the vintage, while its fruit leads; a ripe vintage holds a little longer.
wine.serve: 16 to 17 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; no need to decant; a large red wine glass, with roast kid or lamb.

label.means: The house's name for its old vine Monastrell from the high north of Yecla.
The denomination of origin of one municipality alone, in the north of Murcia.
Organic: by the house's account Hécula has come from organic vineyards since the 2019 vintage.

records.table: Hécula is Bodegas Castaño's Monastrell from old vines in Campo Arriba, the high limestone land north of Yecla. Fermented in steel and given about six months in French and American oak, it is plummy, warm and silky, a red for roast kid or lamb.
records.story: The founder set up Bodegas Castaño in Yecla in 1950 to make his own wines, and from the start, by the house's account, he worked with Monastrell, the grape of the town's own vineyards. On 19 May 1975 a ministerial order approved the rules of the Denominación de Origen Yecla and its Consejo Regulador, an appellation of one municipality alone, whose high northern land, Campo Arriba, was given over to Monastrell. Until then the grape had gone mostly into bulk wine, and it was in the 1980s, by merchants' accounts, that the family began to bottle wine under its own name, and Monastrell of quality in bottle opened the way for others in the town. Hécula, the house's Monastrell from old vines in Campo Arriba, has been on the market for more than twenty years by the house's account. In time the founder's three sons took charge of the vineyards, the cellar and the sales, and with the 2019 vintage Hécula came for the first time from vineyards certified organic, in February 2021. For a sommelier Hécula teaches Yecla in one glass: a single grape, high limestone vineyards and a short time in wood.

report: Searches for this record: 9 of the group's share of 35 (one on the town's name, one on the founder's status, one on the film), no fetch tried; the house's own site was read through search on bodegascastano.com.

The plan's note is answered in part: 1950 and the founder stand on the house's own page and a guide; the founder is named by the house, but no dates and no death were found, so he is described, not named, and he may be living.

The meaning of Hécula as an old name of Yecla, in the plan's why, was not borne out: searches on the town's name give Yakka, the Andalusi fortress, and a pre Roman root, and no source read ties Hécula to the town's name, so the record gives no meaning.

The 1980s for the first bottlings rest on merchants (Enterwine, Liberty Wines and a retailer, one giving 1980), not on the house; Hécula's six months in French and American oak and its vines of about forty years at about 750 metres are the house's notes on the organic 2019 vintage, and the house's product page advises 16 to 17 degrees Celsius.

Left out for want of a second source: a listing of the 1997 vintage of Hécula (wein.plus alone), that Hécula appears in the film Parasite (the house's own blog alone), the Pozuelo vineyard (one merchant), the vineyard area, and the claim that the house was the first in Yecla to move from bulk to bottled wine (one shop).
The region record's producers line calls Castaño Yecla's leading family house whose wines define the denomination for most drinkers; the record leaves the ranking out, and the plan's why repeats it.

wine.name: Olivares Dulce Monastrell
wine.grapes: Monastrell alone, from the estate's oldest ungrafted vines.
wine.sites: The Hoya de Santa Ana estate in the north west of the Jumilla denomination, at about 825 metres, with ungrafted bush vines in sandy loam rich in lime.
wine.making: The oldest vines are left to keep their fruit well into autumn, until the bunches begin to raisin, and they are picked by hand in late October or early November, in about five or six years a decade by the house's account. Fermentation starts with native yeasts on the skins and is stopped with added alcohol to keep the sugar; the wine is bottled without wood the following June.
wine.glass: Cherry red with carmine and maroon tones; an intense, fresh nose of figs, dates and very ripe fruit; in the mouth velvety, full and sweet, long, with a freshness that keeps it from cloying.
wine.ageing: Released after about two years in bottle, it is a young sweet red at its most vivid while its fruit is fresh, and it holds for some years more.
wine.serve: 14 to 16 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small wine glass, with chocolate desserts or blue and aged cheeses, as the house suggests.

label.means: Sweet Monastrell: here a sweet red whose fermentation is stopped with added alcohol.
The denomination of origin of the Monastrell country of inland Murcia.
The half litre bottle in which the house sells its sweet red.

records.table: Olivares Dulce Monastrell is a sweet red from the family's ungrafted bush vines at about 825 metres in the north west of Jumilla, picked late as the grapes raisin and stopped with added alcohol. Pour a small glass with dark chocolate or blue cheese.
records.story: The founder, convinced that Monastrell could make wines of character from this land, began in 1930 to make small quantities of wine for his own district, and so, by the house's account, Bodegas Olivares was born. Around 1960 his sons took on the family winery and sold its wine across Spain. For years the family also made a sweet red for itself and its friends, kept for special occasions, from the oldest vines of its Hoya de Santa Ana estate, ungrafted bush Monastrell high in the north west of the denomination. Jumilla had a long tradition of mistelas, but in 1996, by the house's account, the family made a sweet wine of Monastrell from those vines, and its first commercial release came in 1998; the house tells it as proof that sweet reds of quality could be made there too. Around 2000 the house turned to dry reds as well, and with the new century came Altos de la Hoya. The Dulce is made only in years when the old vines carry their fruit far enough into autumn to raisin, about five or six a decade by the family's count. For a sommelier it is the bottle that teaches Dulce Monastrell: Monastrell left long on the vine, then fortified to keep its sugar.

wine.name: Barahonda Campo Arriba
wine.grapes: Monastrell for the larger part, with Syrah and a little Garnacha Tintorera.
wine.sites: Vineyards of Campo Arriba, the northern and highest land of Yecla, at about 700 to 900 metres, on stony limestone with some sand.
wine.making: The grapes are fermented in stainless steel tanks for about two weeks, and the wine is then aged in French oak barrels, about eight months by the importer's recent sheet; the house's own page for an earlier vintage gave three months.
wine.glass: Blackberry, blueberry and raspberry, a light touch of cinnamon and a chalky note; rich, full bodied and spicy in the mouth.
wine.ageing: Ready on release, it drinks well over its first few years, and a ripe vintage holds for several more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though it gains from being opened half an hour ahead; a large red wine glass, with roast kid or grilled lamb.

records.table: Campo Arriba is Bodegas Barahonda's red from the high limestone north of Yecla: Monastrell for the most part, with Syrah and a little Garnacha Tintorera, aged some months in French oak. Dark berried and warm, with a touch of cinnamon, it suits roast kid or grilled lamb.
records.story: The Candela family tells its story from 1850, when an ancestor began to sell small quantities of wine in Yecla. In 1925, by the house's account, his son founded a small winery, and later generations grew it into a business; the house counts its centenary from that year and marked it in 2025 with a limited bottling of Monastrell from Campo Arriba. Campo Arriba was marked out for Monastrell early: when a ministerial order approved the rules of the Yecla denomination in 1975, its high zone, Campo Arriba, was given over to that grape. In 2006 the fourth generation founded Bodegas Barahonda to raise the quality of the family's wine, with the Monastrell of Campo Arriba at its heart. Zona Zepa, from own rooted vines of more than ninety years there, followed with the 2008 vintage. Campo Arriba, the blend of Monastrell with Syrah and Garnacha Tintorera named for the subzone, is the red by which merchants abroad know the house, sold in some markets as Old Vines. For a sommelier it teaches the subzone on the label: Yecla's higher, stonier north, where the family's vines of more than ninety years grow.

report: Searches for this record: 4 of the group's share of 35, no fetch tried; the house's own site was read through search on barahonda.com.

The plan's note is answered in part: the wine is still made (the 2022 vintage is listed by merchants and the LCBO) and is sold abroad as Campo Arriba Old Vines, in French speaking Canada as Vieilles Vignes; it is a blend, about seven tenths Monastrell with Syrah and Garnacha Tintorera on two merchants' sheets, so the record calls it a Monastrell led blend; 1925 and 1850 are the house's own years.

Planting of 1940 not borne out: the importer Olé & Obrigado dates the vines of Campo Arriba to plantings of 1987 to 1992, which sits uneasily with Old Vines on the label; the record gives no age, and the plan's old Monastrell is left to the integrator.
Founded is 1925, the year the house counts its centenary from; Bodegas Barahonda itself was founded in 2006 by the fourth generation, on the house's own page, and the record keeps both.

The oak: three months in French oak on the house's page for an earlier vintage, eight months on the importer's and a merchant's for recent ones; the record gives eight with the earlier three beside it. The glass draws on a merchant's and a reviewer's notes.

Possible swap for the checker, not proposed: Zona Zepa, from own rooted vines of more than ninety years in Campo Arriba (first made in 2008), or Heredad Candela, the house's old vine Monastrell, would teach old Monastrell more truly than Campo Arriba; Campo Arriba is kept as the wine the house is known by abroad, as the thin region rule allows.

Living people met and not named: the two members of the fourth generation who founded Bodegas Barahonda in 2006, and the founder's grandson who grew the family winery, whose status is unsettled; the ancestors of 1850 and 1925 are named by the house without dates and are described; listed for the read together agent.
Not in WINE_PRODUCERS.
